en: The Sūtra on the Past Deeds of the Bodhisattva Nāgadatta, translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Dharmarakṣa of the Yuezhi during the Western Jin Dynasty.
Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at the Āmrapālī Grove in Vaiśālī, together with a great assembly.
The assembly consisted of twelve hundred and fifty disciples of the Buddha, five thousand bodhisattvas, and countless devas and humans.
At that time, as the Buddha preached the sutra, the entire congregation was settled in meditative concentration.

The Bodhisattva Longshi stood before the Buddha and let out a lion’s roar, extolling the Mahāyāna and recounting his past lives. Having accumulated merit and virtue through successive eons, he had not begrudged his own body or life, nor did he harbor notions of self, seeking nothing for himself. He addressed the Buddha, saying:
“In a past age, there was a Pratyekabuddha dwelling beneath a grove of trees who practiced the Way with diligent application, his mind free from attachment;
he constantly took pity on the people of the ten directions and all crawling creatures, practicing the four immeasurable minds— loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity—
and he always ate fruits and melons while drinking spring water.”
They do not crave worldly glory and have nothing for which they feel greed or attachment;
having attained the five supernormal powers (*pañcābhijñā*), they find delight therein. What are these five?
His eyes could see through solid objects, his ears could hear through all things, and his body could fly; he understood the faculties of others and knew the origins and ends of all things.
Remaining in the mountains, he recited and studied the meaning of the sutras, never flagging day or night.
At that time, there was a venomous snake who, seeing Pañcasikha reciting the sutras day and night, felt great joy in his heart; he approached Pañcasikha, prostrated himself, and paid him homage.
He gathered grass for sweeping and held water in his mouth to sprinkle upon the ground, serving the practitioner with a spirit of never-slackening diligence.

He remained constantly at the practitioner's left side, listening to the sutras without ever departing, and he would immediately recite from memory every sutra spoken by Pañcaśikha, such as those concerning the venomous snake.
Thus, as several months passed and winter’s cold set in, the trees, flowers, and fruits were gradually exhausted.
Pañcaśikha thought to himself:
"Winter has arrived and the flowers and fruits are gone; there is nothing left to rely upon."
"I shall now return and dwell among humans.
Having taken up his robes and bowl, he was about to set out when the venomous snake saw him.
Weeping with grief, its tears fell as it addressed the practitioner, saying:
"Where do you intend to go? The practitioner replied, "The cold season is approaching, yet we have no shelter;
furthermore, the flowers and fruits are exhausted, leaving us with no means to sustain ourselves. Therefore, we are parting ways and wish to enter the commanderies and kingdoms."
Upon hearing this, the venomous snake was moved by even greater sorrow and said to the practitioner:
"With you here, I am like one relying on Mount Tai; day and night I delight in the Dharma, and my mind does not waver."
"Now that you have abandoned me and departed, I am left with no one to rely upon.
I pray you will take pity on me; my body is truly pitiable!
The practitioner replied:
"I possess the four great elements and must always provide food and clothing for them to remain established.
Now, in these mountains there are no provisions; though I have a compassionate heart, I cannot act with autonomy."
The venomous snake said:
"Now, in this mountain, the trees reach toward the heavens, the spring waters flow, and the hundred birds warble; it is truly a place of great delight."
Why do you abandon me? I only pray that the Master will not cast me aside.
Although I must now depart, I wish to follow after you and serve the Master; I dare not remain here, for I am filled with sorrowful thoughts and have nothing but the fear of death.
The practitioner replied:
"You are like a venomous snake, loathed by all people.
Those who see you wish to harm you; no one feels affection or joy toward you."
Or perhaps on the road, tigers, wolves, venomous insects, flying birds, and running beasts will all together harm your body.
Now, in truth, I am filled with deep sorrow that knows no end; though I have such a heart, I cannot attain mastery over it.
"I pray that you remain here, contemplate the Way and keep virtue in mind, maintain yourself with diligence, and endure all hardships!
If you remain strong and healthy as before, we shall meet again in years to come."
The practitioner wept with compassion, but wiped away his tears and departed.
The venomous snake’s tears fell incessantly, unable to stop themselves.
His greed to behold the practitioner knew no end; he immediately climbed a tree and gazed at the practitioner from afar.
He watched as if walking, observing where [the practitioner] was avoiding;
when the practitioner did not appear, he moved further upward;
when he again did not appear, he climbed to the very top of the tree and looked afar at the practitioner, who had by then gone so far that he was no longer visible.
The venomous snake felt even greater compassion and reproached itself, saying in regret:
"This is caused by the transgressions of my own body; I have lost this person of virtuous conduct.

In previous lives, I was foolish and committed many evils—lust, anger, ignorance, negligence, indolence, and lack of knowledge; I did not practice diligence, and my confusion never ceased, for my mind was not unified."
Not encountering the era of a Buddha, they remain far removed from the True Dharma; having lost great wisdom, they stray from ultimate illumination.
Passing from suffering into further suffering, they depart from the *pāramitās* and fall among the five realms of existence as insects, moths, fleas, and lice.
Now that I have received this serpent body and am loathed by others, all of this is due to the faults of my own body and does not stem from others.
Even the noble and wealthy status of the heavens and the human world is impermanent; how much more so this poisonous body of mine?
"Revolving through birth and death is like a chariot wheel.
At that time, the venomous snake spoke of its own faults; its body and mind became tranquil, and it merely reproached itself:
"This perilous body is not worth coveting or cherishing; disregarding my own life and limb, I shall have no attachment here."

He then threw himself down from the tree; before he had even reached the ground, he fell between the branches of the tree, his body severed in two, and he immediately passed away. He was reborn in the Tuṣita Heaven, where he beheld a great radiance.

He then reflected within himself and recognized his past lives: "In my previous existence, I was a venomous serpent. I served a practitioner of the Way, practicing what is right and distancing myself from evil. I was diligent and untiring, subduing the demon of the wicked mind, regarding my own body and life as mere dust and sand."
"Realizing that life is impermanent, he threw himself beneath a tree.
Having ended his life there, he has now been reborn here above.
Then, from among the celestial maidens and the sons of gods in the heavens, each holding fragrant flowers, they scattered them over the venomous snake and spoke these words:
"Although this serpent's body is poisonous and evil, it has been exceedingly kind to me; it shall never be ungrateful.
I shall practice the Dharma with diligent application, my mind free from all attachment."
"Having ended his lifespan, he attained rebirth as a deva.
Now he has descended here specifically to repay his debt of gratitude.
He then proceeded to the place where Pañcaśikha was, prostrated himself in salutation, made offerings of flowers and incense, and praised his meritorious virtues, all of them joining in acclaim:

"Now this practitioner of the Way has no equal; he practices great compassion without distinction between kin and stranger, instructing all beings so that they may leave the three miserable realms behind."
Originally a venomous serpent, [the Buddha] regards me as his own infant; he is concerned for all beings.
This merit is vast, and though I wish to repay his kindness, when will I ever be able to do so?
As soon as he had spoken these words, he returned and ascended to the Tuṣita Heaven.
Accompanied by all the devas, he proceeded before Maitreya;
together they prostrated themselves in worship, their minds entirely equanimous.
Seeing Maitreya, they rejoiced; having completed their prostrations, they stood to one side.
Maitreya preached the Dharma for them, and they all attained the realization of the non-arising of phenomena.
After their lifespans ended in the heavens, they were reborn in this world.
The householder Suvīra had a daughter of exceptionally clear mind,
named Nāgadattā, who had cast off all sensual desires.
At that time, the Buddha came to her home and emitted a brilliant light from between his eyebrows.
At that time, the woman was in the bathhouse, her mind struck with sudden alarm;
she immediately went up to the upper story to look and saw the Buddha’s perfect merits,
his faculties entirely tranquil and composed, and the thirty-two marks clearly manifest.
The woman’s heart was immediately filled with joy;
having now attained peace and security, she resolved to make offerings to the Buddha and the Dharma, and thus gave rise to the bodhicitta.
When Māra heard of this, his heart was filled with sorrowful anxiety.
"This woman has resolved her mind upon the Way; she is one who exhausts the limits of my realm.
Having said this, he transformed himself back into his father and recounted in detail the hardships and afflictions:
"The Buddha now dwells in the world; his merit is most sublime and extraordinary."
"A Bodhisattva undergoes much toil and suffering, while an Arhat is attained quickly and easily.
At that time, the woman replied:
"The Buddha's wisdom is like space, while an Arhat is like a mustard seed."
"Judging from this, the minor paths have no eminent sages;
the Buddha’s virtue is like the vast ocean, delivering beings without end.
At that time, Māra said to the woman:
"Why are you so foolish now? The Bodhisattva undergoes such great hardship that there is no fixed time for him to attain the Way.
If you wish to become a Buddha, you must not begrudge your own life;
by throwing yourself from this tower to the ground, you will then know the woman’s wondrous excellence."
"Through diligence free from attachment, one may attain unsurpassed correctness.
At that time, the woman stood by the railing and, with palms joined toward the Buddha, said:
"For the sake of all beings, may the Buddha know my sincerity."
She then threw herself from the top of the tower, and having attained the state of non-arising, she transformed into the form of a man.
Ānanda was struck with fear and alarm; he joined his palms, adjusted his robes, and stepped forward to address the Buddha, the God among Gods:
"Now my mind is greatly perplexed; what is this? All are utterly deluded;
I pray that the Buddha will manifest great illumination.
Then the Buddha addressed Ānanda:
"Do you see this woman?
Having cast herself into the void, she has transformed into a male body.
Not only has she abandoned her physical form now, but she did so in previous lives as well."
Having already served ten thousand Buddhas, With diligence that never slackened,
In a future age to come, He shall make offerings as numerous as the sands of the Ganges;
He shall then attain Buddhahood, Named Longshang (Dragon-Supreme).
In the first great assembly, he delivered and liberated all devas and humans;
their number is difficult to recount, comparable to drifting clouds.
At that time, when the Buddha governed the world, there was unsurpassed joy and happiness.
Food and drink were all spontaneous, like those in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven.
Thereupon, Nāgadatta, having offered his body, stood before the Buddha and addressed his parents, saying:
"Allow me to become a śramaṇa.
His parents immediately granted him permission; five hundred attendants and eight hundred devas all gave rise to the unsurpassed resolve.
At that time, Māra was filled with sorrow and poison, his remorse and regret beyond expression.
Nāgadatta addressed the Buddha, saying:
"To sever the twelve oceans and eliminate all bitter suffering,"
Because he employs many who are ignorant and deluded, he speaks much of great treasures.
Then the Buddha preached the Dharma, and five hundred of his attendants all attained the state of non-arising.
And eight hundred devas attained the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).
At that time, Nāgadatta stood before the Buddha and spoke of his own past conduct:
"In seeking the Way, I was exceedingly diligent and arduous; it was because I did not cherish my own body."
It was solely for the sake of all people;
the merits of the Tathāgata cannot be fully described or recounted.
At that time, Pañcaśikha was none other than the World-Honored One himself.
That venomous serpent’s body was, in this present life, the body of Nāgadatta;
those five hundred jade maidens were these five hundred people;
and those eight hundred sons of gods shared an incomparable resolve.
Even if one were to have a cause for it, wishing to extol his meritorious virtues,
one could never reach the end.
When he utters the lion’s roar, countless devas and humans—
All gave rise to the unsurpassed truth, and everyone was filled with joy;
they prostrated themselves before the Buddha.
From the *Buddha-bhāṣita-nāgadatta-bodhisattva-pūrvaprabhava-sūtra*.
